utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President. I think the last issue yesterday was the question I had put to the witness, whether in relation to P1013, the order that was given by General Gotovina pursuant to the order of the chief of the Croatian army staff, whether that's an order General Gotovina could have given in his own right or whether this was just following the order of the chief of the Croatian army staff. I believe there was an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was an objection. That objection is overruled. You may put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, could you please ask -- can you please respond to my question.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I mentioned yesterday that P1013 does not allow to draw any conclusions on that issue; however, when we look at Article 61 of the Code Of Discipline -- and if you want I can explain the article; otherwise, I will just summarise it. The Article 61 says that the authorised officer can take any measures he considers necessary to investigate breaches or violations of military discipline. This is discussed on English page 173 in my report, part 1. On English page 182, I include two examples of orders by General Gotovina in relation to the enforcement of discipline where he orders to establish -- among the measures, he orders to establish commissions to investigate violations or breaches. Those can be found on English page 182 and English page 183. I'm referring there to 65 ter 1783 and Exhibit P1019.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Let's go back to the exhibit at hand, P1013.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we can move to the -- to page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, this is obviously a follow-up of what we discussed before. Can you tell us the significance, if any, of this order, again of General Gotovina, on the 8th -- on the 9th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's the 29th of August, not the 9th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. The English translation is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from being wrong, will you take care that a good translation will be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, based on what we see on the screen, I mean, this is the 8th of September. This is the follow-up order 8th of September following the initial order of 29th of August. Do you wish to address me the 8th of September order or the 29th of August one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's the one we see on our screen.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Indeed, Your Honours, on the 8th of September, General Gotovina informs the chief of the HV Main Staff, General Cervenko, of the measures he has taken following this -- the initial order by General Cervenko. The measures are discussed. Of interest is in this context at paragraph 7 or title 7, which is on the English page 5 -- I apologise. I was looking at another document. I was looking at the report Gotovina sends to Cervenko. But following that report, there's also an order by Gotovina which we're looking at now. The problem is there is a combination of documents under one ERN, so I apologise. I retract what I said earlier. Here, Gotovina issues orders to his subordinates, and those are the 4th Guards Brigade -- members of the 4th Guards Brigade and members of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, where he orders the command of 4th Guards Brigade to impose disciplinary measures against the troops under his authority. And for the 72nd Military Police Battalion is concerned, there, Gotovina orders that the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion shall file criminal charges to the military prosecutor's office in Split. Now, there appears to be a distinction in the treatment by Gotovina between the members of the 4th Guards and the members of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, because we're talking about the same type of violation; namely, the illegal occupation of apartments. I connect this distinction in the treatment between these two units to Article 31 of the Code of Discipline, whereby the commander, if he considers that the violation also includes elements of a crime -- and we have to take into account the members of the 72nd Military Police Battalion have the authority of policemen. So it's logical, at least from a military point of view, that Gotovina is more severe when he deals with members of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. So based on Article 31 of the Code of Discipline, Gotovina can order that criminal proceedings should be launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask for clarification because the question was non-responsive, and I have no idea what was just said. Although, let me say that the entire direct has been moving in a manner that gets us to non-responsive questions, because it's just a question of, Tell us what the significance of this is, which is a very broad question, which allows the witness to have wide, wide latitude to start speaking. I'm not sure what the last answer was or what it was an answer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked him to tell us the significance of this order which we see on the screen which has a direct impact on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, before we go to the significance, that the witness tells us how he understands exactly what this order brings us, and I see that he has then put it in a certain legal context. That first question that I put, would that meet some of your concerns?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But there's a whole two or three sentences there which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's perhaps first analyse what is in the document, what exactly is ordered by whom to whom and in respect of what.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Theunens, who is issuing the order, to whom, and in relation to what?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as we can see from the contents of the document and the signature at the end of the document, we see that this is an order issued by General Ante Gotovina, commander of the Split Military District. He issues that order to - and we can see, I mean, not only from the list of addressees, but also from the contents - to the commander of the 4th Guards Brigade, and I refer, therefore, to paragraph 1(A); as well as to the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, which can be found in paragraph 1(B). In those two paragraphs, he also explains what should be ordered, i.e., in 1(A), he orders the command of the 4th Guards Brigade to impose discipline measures under his authority. And in 1(B), he orders the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion to file criminal charges through his specialist staff to the military prosecutor's office in Split. In paragraph 2 of the document, Gotovina then specifies against whom or against which members of the 4th Guards Brigade, as well as of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, and the 73rd Military Police Battalion, the measures he had explained in paragraph 1 should be imposed. In paragraph 3 of the order, Gotovina instructs that his order is to be carried out immediately after returning from combat zone to the barracks. He also orders the commander of the 72nd and the 4th Guards Brigade to report to him on the outcome, i.e., on the implementation of the order, not later than the 31st of October. Paragraph 4 simply explains that Gotovina holds the command of the 4th Guards Brigade and the 72nd Military Police Battalion responsible for carrying out his order, which is in line with the doctrine, what we explained yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, could I ask one question from Mr. Theunens. Mr. Theunens, I see that in 1, under (A) and (B), the commanding officers of the 4th Guards Brigade and the 72nd Military Police Battalion are addressed apparently in relation to the behaviour of members, and we find that in 2, the 4th Guards Brigade, the 72nd Military Police Battalion, but also the 73rd Military Police Battalion. Now, your explanation, more or less, is that 1(A) corresponds with 2(A), and then 1(B) corresponds with 2(B). But then I have difficulties in understanding who should take action against 2(C), because there's no corresponding person or commanding officer addressed in relation to that, which for me raises the question whether the criminal charges under 1(B) are limited to the one member of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, or whether that would include the 73rd. So the structure of this order is not entirely clear to me at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the 73rd Military Police Battalion is not an establishment unit of the Split Military District. It normally belongs to the navy. However, before the start of Operation Storm, it is subordinated to the Split Military District, whereby General Lausic, the chief of the military police administration, appoints Major Juric to organise the subordination of the 72nd and 73rd Military Police Battalion to the Split Military District. There is a specific order for that which is discussed in part 2 of the report. I'm not in a position to establish whether on the date of this order, the 8th of September, 1995, the 73rd Military Police Battalion is still subordinated to the Split Military District. If it still is, then, well, it may - It's sort of like speculation, but I am trying to analyse the order - it may well be that Gotovina expects that the 72nd -- the command of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, through what is described elsewhere in my report as the professional line, i.e., for specialised arms like, for example, military police, there is not only the vertical subordination or operational subordination and operational line of reporting, but there's also a professional line of reporting going through the military police chain from top of the military police administration towards bottom, the individual battalions. So one option is that Gotovina expects the command of the 72nd to inform the 73rd. That would also assume that the 73rd is still subordinated to the -- to the Split Military District. I draw that conclusion because if the 73rd was still subordinate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you there. You said "one option is," and then you say, "I draw this conclusion." Do you opt for that one and are you explaining why, and will you then explain why you reject any other option?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. President. I should have been more precise. In my view, if the 73rd was not subordinated any more to the Split Military District, then General Cervenko would have ordered the navy to take measures in relation to any violations of military discipline by members of the 73rd Military Police Battalion. So I stand corrected for the confusion I may have created in my initial answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, we see that the first order from General Gotovina dates 29th August, 1995, and the last one you just discussed is 8 September 1995. What's the significance of the time-frame here, if any?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we can draw any specific conclusions from that. The issue of the illegal occupation of flats is not a matter, I would say, of operational urgency. So the -- the time period of a bit more of a week to take care of the matter seems to be reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to the next document, which is 65 ter 1292.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is a document dated 27 February 1995 from General Gotovina to the command personally, but at least on page 5 several units; and the subject is "The annual analysis of the state of order, work, discipline, and unusual incidents."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to paragraph 4 on page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Here, it says, and I quote: "The purpose of the analysis is to use concrete indicators for 1994 to establish the basic reasons why an unacceptably large number of unusual incidents (away from the front line) occurred, in which people were killed or wounded with serious consequences or in which extensive material damage was brought about. The unusual incidents that have occurred should be placed in the context of the state of order, work, and discipline in that unit." And in paragraph 6, it details these incidents or breaches that had occurred. The order is addressed, and we see that on page 5, to the 72nd Military Police, among various other units; and at the end, we have a programme of analysis, pages 7 and 8. Mr. Theunens, in relation to command and control and the enforcement of the military discipline, what is the significance, if any, of this document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we know from Article 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just make an objection. I'm not sure what the question, in relation to command and control, what's the significance. If we could have more specific question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you asked several times what the significance is. Of course, it very much depends on what you're looking at. If you could be more precise and more focused in the question on a certain matter, as you did with the last answer; for example, the time-frame, where the witness said the time-frame seems not be a major issue. But could you please guide the witness? That certainly might result in a more effective use of our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In relation to the way General Gotovina used his command and control during that period of time pre-Storm and apparently issued detailed instructions of what has to be done, how do you comment on what's within the prerogative of a commander in order to maintain discipline in his subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object just to the first part of the question which is leading, in the sense it says "used his command and control." As the Court itself has made clear earlier on in the case, there is a difference between operational command and control, and that difference and foundation has not been established with this witness yet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe we established that the witness has experience in the issues of command and control as it relates to the way it's exercised, based on his experience, based on the review of these documents; and he can certainly say what the significance of these instructions here by General Gotovina in February is as to the way command and control has to be exercised in this matter. That's clearly within the experience, training, and skill of Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a separate issues that we all know about, which is the challenge to the qualifications of this witness on command and control. What I am talking about is specifically in the way the question was phrased, it assumes that General Gotovina has command and control over, and in particular Mr. Waespi went out of his way to highlight, the 72nd Military Police, which is highly disputed in this case. So if he wishes to establish foundation for that unit of command and control, then he should do it and not assume it in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, in the question, it is assumed that in one way or another he did or did not exercise command and control, it means the way he used this leaves all relevant aspects open; and, of course, the witness is expected then, if he relates it to the way in which General Gotovina used his command and control, to explain clearly what he means in this respect. Therefore, the witness may answer the question, but is invited to keep in the back of his mind what Mr. Misetic said. Usually, I do not invite witnesses to analyse objections when answering a question. But, Mr. Theunens, I think that you're sufficiently equipped to make that -- to include that in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. As we have seen yesterday, Article 4 of the service regulations of the Croatian armed forces established the duties of commanders. Among these duties are that he is responsible for discipline. This specific document which is sent to -- to prepare a meeting which will cover or will deal with the annual analysis of the state of order, work, discipline, and unusual incidents is a tool for the commander in order to familiarise himself with the situation in his subordinate units, i.e., the units under his command and control; as well as to communicate with these units' commanders about the problems they may have, exchange ideas; and, last but not least, prepare for himself measures, if such measures are necessary, to improve the situation. Also because of the previous document, but this document clearly shows -- and, again, I refer to the Law on Defence where one of the principles of command and control is the unity of command and control, i.e., there's only one commander at a time. I assume we will later address the military police regulations where the issue of command and control, as well as management of the military police, will be addressed. But staying at this order, the fact that the 72nd -- the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion is among the list of participants, i.e., among the addressees, as well as all the other subordinate commanders of the command of the Split Military District, confirms that at that moment in time the 72nd Military Police Battalion is subordinated to the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P1120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1120 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let's move on to the next document, which is 65 ter 1783.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is a document dated 18th March 1995, again by General Gotovina, and again for the -- to the commander personally, and has on page 6 and 7 in the English version a list of units. Let me first ask you, on page 7 where we see 72nd Military Police Battalion, what's the significance of this entry, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the addressees, including the 72nd Military Police Battalion, are at that moment in time subordinate units of the Split Military District commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, how does this document relate to the previous one?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document actually addresses the last item of my reply in relation to the aim of such an annual analysis. In this order, the commander of the Split Military District, General Gotovina, issues a number of instructions, 15 of them, in order to improve discipline and order in the units of the Split Military District. I would like to draw attention to the third instruction Gotovina gives, that is -- sorry, which can be found on English page 2, where Gotovina orders that: "For each unusual incident within Split Military District units that results in a death or serious injury, unit commanders shall form a commission tasked with investigating the case and sending a report to the Split Military District command operations centre." I highlight that in context of the earlier questions about whether or not the commander of a military district has the power to establish a commission that deals with disciplinary issues or disciplinary investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1121, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1121 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the last document in this section, Mr. President, is 65 ter 3558.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 31st of May, 1995, authored by General Gotovina, and it addresses problems in the Split 306th Logistics Base; and in the order, several issues, measures, are taken. Paragraph 1, I quote: "The commander of the 306th Logistics Base shall urgently take measures -- necessary measures in order to establish order, improve work and discipline, and introduce proper soldierly relations in the 306th Logistics Base and its sections." And item 3: "In addition to general measures, special measures to improve the situation shall be undertaken," and lists several specific measures. Again, Mr. Theunens, the significance of this order to the -- from General Gotovina to the commander of a subordinate unit?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is another example of the implementation by General Gotovina of Article 4 of the service regulations that we can find under D32. Among his responsibilities as a commander is to maintain discipline. Discipline is necessary also to maintain combat readiness; and because of what is described as problems in relation to the issues of order, work, and discipline in one of his subordinate units, he takes measures in order to improve the situation which falls within his authority and duties as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P1122, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1122 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to move on to the second topic, and this is the issue of the military police and the subordination, and you can find relevant parts in paragraph 10 and 46 and 48 in the executive summary. I'd like to quote one conclusion in this executive summary. This is on page 31 English of the report, which is marked for identification 1113 -- it's 1013, I'm told by Mr. du Toit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, while that's being done, I quote from paragraph 46; in B/C/S it's on page 18: "Lausic," and you have already addressed his role, "confirms the subordination for operational matters of the MP to the operational commanders military district and OG, and appoints Major Ivan Juric to assist with command and control over the 72nd and 73rd Military Police Battalion." Based on your analysis, who commanded the military police, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, could you please clarify whether we addressed the situation prior to Operation Storm, i.e., the situation as it is foreseen by doctrine; or do we address the situation during and after Operation Storm; or both?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's first start with the pre-Storm situation. We'll go into documents immediately, but just in very general terms, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The doctrinal instructions that apply to the command and control and management of the military police can be found in Articles 8 and 9 of the 1994 rules on the military police, which, if I'm not wrong, have been tendered here as Exhibit P880.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think that might be a good moment to pull P888 [sic] up. This is on page 5 in the English version and also in B/C/S. P880.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to Article 8, I would like to make a brief comment on the English translation, because the English translation states "command and control." Now, in military language, the word "command" has a very specific meaning and the word "control" has a very specific meaning, as well as the expression "command and control." I have included these definitions in part 1 of the report, the JNA definition, the US armed forces definition, as well as the British definition of command and control, because at the time of the filing of the report, I didn't have a Croatian regulation defining the concept of command and control. These definitions show that control in the sense of command and control does not -- cannot be dissociated from command, i.e., it is one concept. Of course, we can address particular subordination relations that exist in NATO armies, where there can exist something like operational command, which is different from operational control, which means something else than tactical command, which is again different from tactical control. All these expressions have a particular meaning in a sense that they define the responsibilities and the authority of the commander in relations to the forces that are given to him. Again, I don't want to draw this too long because it lacks relevance for the HV, because in the HV, we didn't have the specific subordination relations in 1995, like tactical command or tactical command or operational control or operational control. But, still, I just wanted to mention that to highlight the importance of terminology. The translation in Article 8 states command and control; whereas, in the B/C/S text, we see --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, has the witness now been accredited in B/C/S as well? If so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, well, if there's anything -- he apparently has paid attention to the language. Let him explain, not to say that he is a linguistic expert. Of course, if there's criticism about or if you could challenge that, of course, we could do that. But let him finish his answer, and then we'll see whether there's any merit or value in it, rather than to interrupt him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to make my objection then, because if it's going to be stated that he's also capable of reading the original text, that is not something on his CV, it's not in the report, it should be something that's disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I understand is that this witness has analysed a lot of documents of which the originals are often in B/C/S, and they were translated. And just as everyone here in this courtroom has, now and then, made comments on translations, whether they're complete or not, whether they're missing words, whether there are terms which could be understood in a different way, let's first give an opportunity. It also will give you some insight in how this witness worked. And if it becomes apparent that he's totally wrong with this, I would say, this small element, which certainly is not the core of his expertise but apparently a tool, a tool he used, I take it that he has sought advice on translation issues, as we all do constantly - you less perhaps than we - and then to see what remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if in advance, Mr. Theunens and/or Mr. Waespi were going to challenge the translation of what is not simply a minor issue, the issue of command and control over the military police is central to the Prosecution's case, if there's an issue in the translation, why isn't this brought to our attention and corrected before we get here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Misetic. I think it's a different matter. Translation is a linguistic exercise. If you have different systems, it's not only a matter of translation, but it's also a matter of understanding whether words sufficiently can express differences. That's not just -- it's also conceptual issue. Let me just give you an example. It's clear that if you would translate the term "judgement rendered in absentia" in German, you would have no problem. It's "abwesenheitsurteil," or "judgement of someone that is not there." If you would translate it into French, you would certainly find that there are two different kinds of judgement rendered in absentia in France. So, there, it's not purely a translation issue. It's not "jugement par defaut," but "jugement par contumace." So, there, you see that the difference in structure may have some impact on translation issues. Now, what this witness tells us is that the concepts underlying the language ask for specific caution if we are talking about translating concepts, terms relating to certain concepts. The witness doesn't have to be a linguistic expert to draw our attention to that. Mr. Theunens, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wish to clarify that during the informal meeting with the Gotovina Defence on the 17th or 18th of January, 2008, I, indeed, stated that I do not speak B/C/S, but I have tried, like in the other cases I worked on, to understand or to get a basic understanding of military terminology, because I understand from my training and studies that the correct definitions of terms are the starting point and that there should be clarity about that. What I tried to say is that the term "upravljanje" - and I apologise for the wrong emphasis - in my understanding and based on the context I had, for example, during the Vukovar trial, where we had several issues with translation, in my understanding means "management," "administration." If command and control was meant in Article 8 in the military sense of command and control like it is used in any army, the concept of command and control, then I would have expected the Croatian expression - and again I apologise for the emphasis -"zapovljedanje i vodjenje." When we look at Article 8, it does mention "zapovljedanje," but it uses "upravljanje" instead of "vodjenje." That's something I wish -- I wanted to highlight. In my view, it doesn't have a major impact on the relations between the military police and the military district commander or the military police and the operational commander -- I apologise, the military police and the military police administration commander, on one hand, and the military police and the operational commander, on the other hand. But I think it is useful that we use the correct terminology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we come at a point where the linguistic aspect, how your views on concepts translate to language. Mr. Waespi, we have -- the witness has drawn our attention to these conceptual issues. He then continued to tell us what he would expect the language which would properly express what he said. You and the Defence are invited to see whether the translation as it is here, perhaps with the assistance of linguistic experts, interpreters, to see whether this is a correct translation or not, or at least a correct reflection in English of what the original text tells us. If you can agree on the matter, fine. If you cannot agree on the matter, you're invited to make submissions in which you may rely on linguistic expertise. I expect the parties to agree on what could be considered - let's try not to have lengthy reports by linguistic experts on the matter - but let's see whether the concerns expressed by Mr. Theunens, because that's how I understand it and not the linguistic solution for it, how they may be an obstacle for this Chamber to understand what this text, this Article 8, tells us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just come in here, because it's important in a number of ways. We need to check, of course, Mr. Theunens's sources for his statement in court today; and, obviously, that is the kind of material that would have to be assembled. So we -- we may review his opinion that he's just given, check how it came about that he came to that opinion, and also have the matter reviewed by experts to come in the court. As the Court knows, there will be experts to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I see you're telling us you'll do your homework. But in relation to the invitation I just sent to both parties, has that any practical effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say you need more time to prepare for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, we would need his sources for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. We can ask. You mean the sources on language?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. How he's come to -- yes. He's said because he was in a trial involving Vukovar that there were issues in that trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd like to know in what respect exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what in the Vukovar trial triggered your attention in this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to be as brief as possible, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The matter of management and command and control did not arise directly in the Vukovar trial, but, for example, there were translations like a "referent" were systematically related to a "clerk"; whereas, a "referent" is a B/C/S term for an "officer working in a staff." Well, in English, in my view, it would be a "staff officer." There are, obviously, clerks working in a military staff, but an officer working in a staff is not a clerk, even though he will be called "referent" in B/C/S. There have been minor issues with like, for example, members of the military police were at one moment systematically translated as "military police officers." It is obvious that they are officer in a military police unit like in any other unit, but not every military policeman is an officer, even though in some languages, a member of the police is identified as a police officer. This is not an exercise in trying to be more clever or criticising. Military language can be and is very specific. For example, during staff course and military academy, you spend a lot of time in understanding the right concepts that, for example, when you receive, as a tank company commander, an infantry platoon under tactical control, it will mean something totally different from if you mean -- if you receive that unit under operational command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, this the kind of observations you made, did that trigger your attention? So let me try to understand what the issue is. The issue is that a comparative functional analysis reveals differences or lack of differences which are not always found in the language, that is different language or the same language, when these systems are described? Is that more or less what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. Then in relation to the "upravljanje," I was asked by one of the court translators who knew me, I think from the Vukovar trial, to find out what "management" means the military sense and in the language used here, B/C/S. We have a JNA military lexicon which dates from 1988 -- 1981 - I apologise - where all these terms are described. It's very similar, obviously it's in a different language, but there's also a joint military dictionary, for example. I am aware of the distinctions and the differences between Serbian and Croatian. I'm also aware about the distinctions in military terminology. "Command and Control" in Serbian is "Rukovodjenje i Komandovanje, "RiK." In Croatia, it is "ViZ," "Vodjenje i Zapovjedanje." Again, I apologise for the wrong pronunciation. "Upravljanje" is defined in the JNA military lexicon as "management," and I have the definition here, if you wish. I asked my colleagues for a Croatian military lexicon, but it doesn't seem to be available in the OTP. Now, it would be very useful if such a lexicon exists that we would check in that Croatian military lexicon how "upravljanje" is defined there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, first of all, I invited the witness to tell us what caused him to address the matter, where he said the Vukovar case, it seems to me the kind of problem he describes, that he saw that in the Vukovar case, rather than the language on this issue. Is there any other matter you need for your further homework apart from what the witness told you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. That was very helpful in dealing with the extent of it, at a preliminary stage and as best as we could here, without going into further detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic was on his feet as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I understood the witness directly, he apparently checked on this issue before he came to court or before he began his testimony? Okay. He's nodding his head in agreement. Once again, 750 pages, proofing sheets, addenda, corrections to it. I don't know why issues are being prepared for trial, for direct testimony, that are not being disclosed to the Defence that are going to be dealt with on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know. I think as a matter of fact that Mr. Waespi did not specifically ask about this, but the witness said, "Before I answer the question, I'd like to draw your attention to ..." So he introduced it. If it was on Mr. Waespi's mind already, then, of course, your objection would make sense. But I think the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Topic number 3 is military police command and control. Now, I would think that this issue at some point would come up that: Let my alert you to the fact that we think there's a mistranslation or there's a different interpretation of that language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, were you at all at notice that the witness gave this attention to this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not in that detail. I do remember during proofing when we discussed the article that he said that he thought the language of "management" was an issue, but I didn't explore it any further, and I wasn't meant to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed. Let's proceed at this moment. The invitation for the parties is to agree on the matter or to make submissions, because it seems to be a rather, well, vital issue. The Chamber would like to receive the parties' views on the matter if there's no common view on the matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go into substance of Articles 8 and 9 as it relates to command and control and subordination of the military police. Who commanded the military police prior to Storm, number 1, and during Operation Storm, number 2?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Article 9 stipulates that the military police, while they are performing their regular military police tasks, the military police is subordinated to the operational commander, i.e., it is specified the military district commander or the navy commander or the command of the air force or the highest HV commander by function in the military police unit's area of operations. Article 9 has to be seen in conjunction with Article 8, which states, obviously, that military police are subordinated to the Ministry of Defence military police administration. That's what I tried to explain at the beginning. There are for specialised units, for example, military police, there is what is defined in HV doctrine a professional line and an operational line. At another moment in time, it was described as the horizontal line or the vertical line. It is obvious that issues dealing with, for example, the training of military police, the procedures they apply, their administration, that this has to be centralised in order to achieve and maintain uniformity in these areas, as well as in the activities of the military police, for whatever battalion wherever it is deployed in Croatia or to which whatever military district it belongs. That is the role of the military police administration. Now, when the military police is conducting, is carrying out its tasks, a company, military police company, can be subordinated to a brigade or to an Operational Group. A battalion, like, for example, the 72nd is subordinated to the Split Military District, it means that it is the operational commander for the 72nd Split Military District commander who orders the military police to carry out military police tasks, because you cannot centralise that. It would be impossible for the military police administration to order each and every military police battalion in its daily operations. The same procedure exists in the United States armed forces, where there is, indeed, a force provost marshall, as well as a provost marshal lower echelons, which would correspond with military police administration; however, he serves as an advisor to the operational commander at that level and an advisor in procedural matters like how to use the military police; but it is the operational commander who decides about what to do with the military police when and where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would submit that answer is non-responsive to the question Mr. Waespi posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's not correct. I asked him who command the military police based on his analysis. Looking at these two Articles, he explained the distinction between operational command, on one side, and what he describes as a professional line of reporting very well. I think he perfectly answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the specific question was "prior to Storm number one, and during Storm number two." If that could be clarified, because I think he spoke more in a theoretical framework, rather than the specific questions that Mr. Waespi posed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We will look into right now a few documents that are going to be specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say you will deal with that, although it is not yet -- the distinction is not clearly present in the answer, you will give it follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to the next document which is 3021, 65 ter 3021.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is an order by General Gotovina, dated 25th of July, 1995, and it's addressed to the 72nd Battalion of the military police and the military police of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. It orders, in paragraph 1, that forces of the 72nd Battalion of the military police shall set up check-points and patrols on the left side of the OG North's zone of responsibility with specific locations. And in paragraph 3, it talks about specific tasks of the military police, for instance, to ensure order and discipline, prevent incidents in the aforementioned zone of responsibility, oversee the allowed distance and speed of vehicles, prevent the unlawful use of weapons, the misuse of materiel and technical equipment and other goods. Mr. Theunens, in relation to what is said before in theory, based on the doctrine, what is the significance of this order of General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an example of the implementation of Article 9 of the rules of military police, because we see that the operational commander issues orders on the use of the military police to his military police. I refer specifically to the 72nd Military Police Battalion, because the situation with military police of the so-called Herceg-Bosna republic may very well be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to -- I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P1123.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1123 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let's move to D267, Defence exhibit already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is an order by General Lausic, whom you have mentioned already as the chief of the military police administration. It dates 2nd August 1995. The subject is "Preparations of military police units to perform military police tasks in the areas of responsibility of the Croatian ... military districts during the upcoming operations." I would like to focus on paragraph 3, and it says: "IZMs of VP battalions with all necessary officers and equipment shall be set up at the IZMs of the HV military districts. The required minimum number of officers and amount of equipment shall remain in parent headquarters to ensure that the continuity of work is not interrupted. "Within the daily operational chain of command, commanders of VP battalions shall be subordinated to commanders of the HV ZPs," and it has a deadline. Mr. Theunens, what's the significance of this paragraph in relation to subordination of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour. It's an open-ended question. I'd ask for foundation as if this witness notes what "daily operational" means before the broader question is posed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness include that in his answer, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is another example of the implementation of Article 9, i.e., for the daily or regular military police administrations, military battalions are subordinated to the operational commander. Now, because this order is dated the 2nd of August, this is right before the launching of Operation Storm. We know that the Split Military District has established forward command posts. It is logical, in order to implement or to allow smooth conduct of command and control, that there is a military police presence or military police command presence at the forward command post of the Split Military District, as well as the other military districts in Croatia. Therefore, Lausic orders the military police battalions to set up forward command posts at the forward command posts of the military districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I still don't think the definition of "daily operational" has been established.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, the daily operational of the military police, I would like to refer you, then, to the 1994 rules on the military police, wherein, for example, chapter 3, which is on English page 5 starting at Article 10, the duties of the military police are described in general terms. I have also addressed this in my report starting at part 1, English page 82. If you want to go in more detail, there are also different services within the military police whereby each service has its own specialities. These are also addressed in the 1994 rules, and I have attempted to summarise them in my report. Now, if you want me to go into specifics or read them out, I'm available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's not necessary as long as I understand the witness correctly that he thinks that daily operational tasks are all the tasks that the military police has.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's not really what I said. I have said that the tasks of the military police are described in Article 10; and the tasks listed there, well, the protection of life and the personal security of military personnel and other Republic of Croatia citizens and the protection of their property is, for me, a daily task of the military police. The second, the prevention and uncovering of crimes, as we have also seen from earlier documents we discussed, is a regular military police task. Number 3, ensuring safety of military traffic is a regular military police task. I mean, I can continue read them out, I don't know whether it's efficient use of court time, but I do not rule out that the military police administration can give specific tasks to military police battalions. Some of them may touch upon the regular tasks. However, my understanding from the review of the 1994 rules, as well as of the documents both prior as well as during and after Operation Storm, as well as my prior knowledge on the role and use of military police, is that the military police - that is, the Croatian military police and more specifically the 72nd Military Police Battalion - was subordinated to the command of the Split Military District while carrying out regular military police tasks prior to, during, and after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I see whether I understand the issue. In your answer, you often refer to regular tasks; whereas, I understood Mr. Misetic to seek your views on especially the word "operational."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Operational and, more specifically, daily operational, and it's important for the purposes of being able to prepare for cross-examination to establish what this witness's basis is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Daily operational tasks, that's what Mr. Misetic is seeking your views on, and your answer does not -- uses at least different terms. To the extent you meant the same, please explain it; if not, please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may have confused two issues. I have addressed the regular military police tasks. Well, for me, regular military police tasks are the same as daily military police task; however, I understand that Mr. Misetic wants me to clarify the concept of 'daily operational chain.' I would like to refer to that for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Daily operational task, not daily operational chain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then, yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that the text was read was about daily operational chain or chain of command. The text read was "within the daily operational chain of command, commanders of battalions shall be subordinated to commanders of the HV IZPs." That was the text we were seeing, Mr. Misetic, not daily operational tasks. So could you give us your views on what that exactly means, daily operational chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The operational chain of command is as it is defined in Croatian doctrine is addressed on page 130 of the English -- excuse me, English page 130 of the first part of my report, where I refer to an October 1995 HV regulation, which makes a distinction between commanding along the direct line of command or the regular line, as well as commanding and reporting along the professional or the functional line. I will just read out what I put there, well, because it explains what the operational chain means. It states: "The operational commander directly commands the operational formations, higher tactical units, and service units. The operational commander also exercises command over units that are 'temporarily resubordinated to him or to his subordinate commands.'" If you want, I can also explain the command and reporting along the professional line. It may be useful in the context of military police. The professional line means that, and, again, I'm quoting from a HV regulation: "In addition to the orders they receive from the operational commander, subordinate commands and units can also receive orders from the chiefs of combat branches and services in the staff of the superior operational forces command. The orders that are passed along the professional or functional line," I mean they mean both the same, "deal with specific issues that are relevant for the implementation of the task that has been imposed by the operational commander." I have added there my personal comment: "The existence," for my conclusion, "The existence of the professional line, therefore, does not violate the principle of single and unified command." So coming back to what is put here, daily operational chain of command, it is my conclusion that this is the chain of command along the operational line, i.e., from the Split -- from the chief of the Main Staff to the military district commanders, to the OG commanders, the brigade commanders, battalions, companies, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's then the meaning of the word "daily" rather than "operational" chain of command? Daily operational chain of command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Daily," in my view means, well, regular -- doing operations. They wouldn't -- in my view, there is no need for this word "daily." It is like the regular, the normal, the usual. Daily is not a military expression. I've never seen the expression "daily command."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's quoted here, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that you have you've never seen it is contradicted by the document we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't seen it in other documents. My conclusion is that it doesn't reduce or influence in any way the operational chain of command. It has no influence on the concept of -- on the authority of the operational commander over the military police, as is specified also -- or is established in Article 9 of the 1994 military police rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has explained what he understood. Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to clarify, the term "daily" within daily operational chain of command, I understand your answer is you haven't seen it in a regulation -- in regulation that forms part of the doctrine.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. The word "daily," yeah, I would agree. that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to paragraph 10 of this document, and it deals in paragraph 2 with the appointment of Major Ivan Juric and a group of officers from the regular VP session and VP administration crime section, to assist in commanding and organising the activities of the 72nd VP and 73rd Split VP battalion, that shall perform tasks in its own area of responsibility and provide necessary assistance to the 72nd VP battalion. The commanders of the 72 VP battalion and the 73rd VP battalion shall be subordinated to Major Ivan Juric. You have mentioned it a moment ago, but please explain it again, why based on a review of the materials, your knowledge of the doctrine, Major Juric was appointed to this job.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as explained earlier, the 73rd Military Police Battalion, even though it is located in Split, is not an organic unit of the Split Military District. It belongs normally to the navy. However, for operational reasons, the 73rd Military Police Battalion has been ordered to assist the 72nd Military Police Battalion, i.e., it becomes a unit of the Split Military District. And in order to facilitate command and control and over these two units, a coordinator or -- yeah, a coordinator has been appointed; namely, Major Ivan Juric. This makes it easier both for the military police administration as well as for the command of the Split Military District to give instructions to the military police, as they only have to speak to one person, i.e., Ivan Juric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask for more foundation for this opinion, Your Honour. It's not in the report. Nothing has been disclosed to us on this, and the witness is opining based on his theories without any facts that have been presented or citation to documents. You know, this is, all morning, new opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is an expert. He disclosed his report. He included several opinions on distinct topics. He's clearly entitled to provide these opinions on related areas that are included in these documents. They have been disclosed to the Defence in advance. That is nothing new. That is in line with his expertise, in line with his opinions that he provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, the witness goes further. He draws conclusions so that it's for whom it would be easier to deal in this way. I think there's some merit in the request by Mr. Misetic, that the witness further explains his last answer, that he gives further foundation to his last answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I checked with my colleagues. They are of the same opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can I make one additional point, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In your decision of the 21st May 2008, that was the decision on part of the Gotovina Defence's Rule 73 motion in limine, which addressed a similar issues, you ordered or you decided in paragraph 7: "The Prosecution is obliged to give notice of evidence that it intends to present through proper disclosure. If proper notice has been given, a party may examine an expert witness with respect to matters not included in his or her expert report as long as they are within the knowledge of the witness relevant and probative."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I'm not objecting against the matter you addressed. The issue here is the witness gives a few opinions which seem to be related to the logic of the structure that was put in place, and where these conclusions do not immediately follow from what the witness has told us, Mr. Misetic invites the witness, and through me invites the witness, to give, as I understand it, to give a basis apart from what we have seen in this document. He does not, just as I do not and just as the Chamber does, not prevent you from putting these questions. The Chamber does not object to Mr. Misetic insisting on, already at this stage, finding a foundation going beyond to what the witness has offered us until now. Mr. Theunens, it gave you at least one minute to think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. This order, which is D267, is also discussed in part 2 of my report, English pages 208 to 210, where I agreed that I didn't go -- I didn't explain why Juric is appointed. However, I would like to draw your attention to another order which is discussed on page 210 in my report. This is 65 ter 3111. This is an order from the -- from Lausic further specifying the duties of Major Ivan Juric. I quoted from that document that: "Juric is superior to the commanders of the 72nd and the 73rd Military Police Battalion with regard to the 73rd Military Police Battalion providing assistance to the 72nd Military Police Battalion." The answer I gave to the previous question was based on my experience in such situations, i.e., that in cases of temporary subordinations and temporary grouping of units, it may be useful from the point of view of command and control to appoint a coordinator or to appoint one person who is superior over these two resubordinated units. If you allow me, I can give another example. We know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic was asking for a foundation. Mr. Misetic, the other example you'd like to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, as well as, if I may, where he says "his experience in such situations ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please give your other example to start with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other example is, when we look at the Split Military District order for attack for Operation Kozijak [phoen], or Storm, which is 65 ter 3119, we see that the command of the Split Military District establishes four operational groups. Operational groups do not exist in peacetime, except maybe during exercises. But when we look at the composition of these operational groups, they group different types of forces. There are guards brigades included, there are regular brigades included, there are Home Guard units included, as well as artillery, engineers, and other units. All these different units will operate in the same area, the zone of responsibility of the specific operation group, all with the same mission. Of course, the engineers will not carry out the same specific mission as the infantry, but the overall mission for that operational group will be one and the same. It is logical from the military point of view that instead of having the operational commander, Gotovina, issue an order to each and every individual brigade, battalion, infantry, armour, artillery, and so on, it is much easier to issue orders to the Operational Group commander, who will then issue the orders to his subordinate units. This is exactly the same that is happening here with the military police. Instead of having both Lausic as well as Gotovina having to speak to the commander of the 72nd Battalion and the 73rd Battalion, it's much easier to be in contact with only one person who can also assist them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, it's not for the first time that you referred to Mr. Gotovina as Gotovina. Since Mr. Gotovina is present in this courtroom and whatever language you may use in internal discussions within your team, I think it's basic politeness to address persons who are present, either, as I do by, Mr. Gotovina or, as in the questions put to you by Mr. Waespi, General Gotovina. That would be appreciated, if you would keep that in mind. I think you answered the question. I'm looking at the clock. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have one foundational question and the break will give Mr. Theunens the opportunity on this, but my foundational question based on his last answer is, if he can establish foundation for General Gotovina issuing an order to Mr. Juric. That would help in light of his last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm just wondering whether these are issues for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's a foundation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's foundation, Your Honour, for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's mixed. To some extent, these are matters that could be brought up in cross-examination. At the same time, they are -- for example, this example, the witness has given his foundation, and whether you find it sufficient or not is -- so to that extent could have been kept for cross-examination. At the same time, it certainly assists the Chamber in better following the evidence, better understanding the evidence, and not to wait till what happens in eight or ten days from now. At the same time, I also want to urge the Defence that we should not unnecessarily interrupt the flow of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I get the feeling that as tension at this moment between your need to often find foundation for what the witness says and the need of the Chamber and the need of the other party to have an uninterrupted flow of evidence, it's finding balance. The last example where Mr. Waespi says it could have been kept for cross-examination, where you say it relates to foundation, there's merit in both point of views. Let's try to find a proper balance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. And on the Defence side, we like to get to cross-examination as fast as possible, I assure you. The only reason I rise is on issues that are not addressed in the report or the subsequent filings, I'm just asking for more information, so that we can be prepared for cross-examination as to the basis for these additional opinions that the witness is providing. Otherwise, I agree with you. We do not object on foundation to the matters that are in the report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, if you would pay proper attention to the foundation for the answers you expect the witness to give and to introduce the matter in such a way that no issue of foundation arises, and if the Defence would consider what issues even in respect of foundation could be left for cross-examination if the foundation is not complete or if it's flawed in your view, to what extent it's really necessary to deal with it and interrupt the flow of evidence, then we might together find the balance I think we need at this moment. Mr. Theunens, you've got 25 minutes to think about an answer of the last question that was put to you by Mr. Misetic. We'll have a break, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, the last question, you still remember it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have not included any orders by General Gotovina to Major Juric in my report because I didn't come across such documents while conducting my research. However, I have included documents that indicate that General Gotovina issues orders directly to the 72nd Military Police Battalion, as well as orders indicating cooperation Major Juric and an OG commander, OG Zadar, for example. That is 65 ter 419. I have also included -- I apologise for the transcript. I have also included documents in my report that indicate that, for example, the 3rd Company of the 72nd Military Police Battalion conducts combat operations. That can be found, for example, at page 221 of my report, 65 ter 1072. The fact that a unit of the 72nd Military Police Battalion carries out a combat task or combat operations implies, at least from the military point of view, a subordination relation whereby this company is subordinated to an operational commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of specific tasks then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let's move to the next exhibit, next document, and this is 65 ter 3114.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is an order by General Gotovina, dated 2nd August 1995. The subject line is: "72nd VP military police battalion," and it deals with mobilisation. "Order: Mobilise to full strength. Time of mobilisation: Immediately." Mr. Theunens, please tell us the significance, if any, of this specific order to mobilise the 72nd VP in Split for the subordination of this unit.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document shows that on the 2nd of August, the 72nd Military Police Battalion is a unit of the Split Military District and is subordinated to General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit P1124, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit P1124 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Waespi, if the witness makes reference to a certain document in his answer under a 65 ter number, I wonder whether it would not be wise that in order to understand his answer, that it be made available; and if it's a 65 ter number, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We were planning to include that in a list of documents tendered from the bar table at the end of his testimony. We assume that the Defence will use quite a number of these documents in their cross-examination, so our plan was to wait until the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't necessarily have a problem -- I don't have a problem with whatever document he specifically referenced. I just wondered in light of your order about how you wanted us to approach the documents, and since we're waiting on guidance from the Trial Chamber, in other words, you clearly stated in your order, you didn't want us to be putting in a lot of documents from the report, unless they're specifically disputed or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, disputed. Here, apparently, in a specific question put to the witness, he relies on a certain document for his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There, of course, there is, I would say, there is a need for the Chamber to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was unclear. What I'm saying is I agree with you. I have no objection to that. I am speaking now to the issue of a bar table coming at the end. That may be what the issue is in light of your order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understood the bar table aspect here to be that it's saved for a rainy day, and that we then get them all together, instead of having them introduced one by one through the witness. The disadvantage, Mr. Waespi, is that we are deprived from an opportunity to look at the documents when we're still hearing the evidence of this witness, because it's not accessible for us. So, therefore, perhaps you could -- if you could produce that list in an ongoing fashion so that the documents can already be assigned a number, if only being marked for identification, but that at least the Chamber has access to this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, and I don't want to belabour this - so perhaps during the next break or afterwards, you can explain it to us - but paragraph 30 of your decision of 17 November 2008 states in the last sentence: "The Prosecution is invited to only tender documents referenced in the expert report which are necessary for such an examination-in-chief." However the Court wishes to deal with it is fine with me, just so that we know in cross-examination whether we're still required per the Court's order to challenge the summaries of the documents even if they're not tendered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll give you guidance on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have to look at it in more detail, also in view of the experience we have at this moment. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just on this point, obviously, in the time given, I can't go through all the documents, the key documents, so I will address at the end the documents that are remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Within the limits of our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. 65 ter 3119.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is the offensive operation order with attachments, dated 2nd August 1995, issued, as we see from page 19 in the English, by General Gotovina. And if we go back to the first page, we see that there is an attachment, number 7, "Security Plan," to which we'll go in a moment. But at this point, I would like to go to page 17, which addresses transportation. That's at paragraph 4 at the bottom. I'll read the relevant part on this page and the next one: "Use establishment motor vehicles for the transportation of personnel, materiel, and equipment. "Send requests for additional transportation of personnel, materiel and equipment to the superior command." Next page in the English: "72nd VP battalion with reinforcements shall be in charge of regulating and controlling traffic."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. This is page 14, 15 in B/C/S, which we have found now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, this paragraph 4, as it relates to the VP section, how is that related to the issue of subordination of the military police 72nd unit to General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this entry in the order for attack shows that the 72nd Military Police Battalion is subordinated to General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender the document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number P1125, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1125 is admitted into evidence. May I ask one question? If I look at this order and if I look at the task assign, if I think about the earlier explanation you gave about the daily operational command, I wouldn't consider this to be a daily matter, but a rather, broad task, where I would expect that orders on where to go, et cetera, that that would be the daily implementation of it, perhaps left to others. I'm just trying to understand. You said the word "daily" operational chain of command was totally superfluous, where I see apparently that sometimes tasks are assigned on a broad sense. Of course, on the basis of this, you wouldn't know where to go, so there must be more. Is that an idiotic thought? Well, apart from that, is that a thought that you would -- Let me phrase it in a better way: Is it something that sounds reasonable to you; or are there any reasons to say, no, that's not a correct distinction you are suggesting?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Your presentation is very correct, if I am allowed to express myself in that way. Two comments. Detailed instructions, for example, the military police but for also the artillery or other units, will be included in the annexes. That brings me to the second comment: This is the offensive order for attack or the order for the offensive operation, which is the first order. It sets the overall framework. I will not use too much time by going through the order, but this is the start of the whole thing, at the level of the Split Military District at least. General Gotovina has received an order from the chief of the Main Staff to conduct an operation. He uses that order to prepare orders for his subordinate units. The first order is the offensive operation order. The template looks very standardised. You start with an overview of the enemy situation. You then, as a commander, you explain the submission you have received. Subsequently, you explain what your unit will do, and this is all done according to particular procedures. Then you explain the orders or the task of the subordinate units. This order is issued on the 2nd of August; however, once the operation is launched, there will be new orders. That's what I have tried to explain in part 1 of the report, when I talk about the command process. Orders are given continuously, and then, of course, in that context, the word "daily" makes sense, because then there will be an order, for example, given at the evening meeting.
