Certain instructions will be issued; that mission will be implemented; there are new situational developments; and, again, these developments, as well as other instructions from the superior command, will bring the commander - in this case, the military district commander - to issue again orders. It's continuously happening. So that hopefully explains the expression "daily."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now we go to the annex that was mentioned by the witness, which is 65 ter 171.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's called Plan Of Security Measures. We see on the first page, on the top left, the approval of General Ante Gotovina, and we see on the last page the deputy commander OG North for SIS, Zeljko Pavic. Now, before we go into details, could you briefly explain what this document is, especially as it relates to the person who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is one of the annexes I mentioned, I mean the annexes to the order for attack. This is the plan of security measures for Operational Group North. As we see in the previously admitted document, General Gotovina has decided to create four OGs: North, Sinj, Sibenik, and Zadar. It should actually be -- it's not the deputy commander, but assistant commander for SIS, so for security and intelligence. Zeljko Pavic, he here in this plan gives instructions to his personnel, i.e., the units of OG North, in order to implement certain measures before combat operations, during combat operations, and after combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Let's go into a couple of entries. The first entry I'd like to refer you to is on page 2, item 7; and that's also on page 2 in the B/C/S version. I quote: "Measures ..." -- the first column as we see from the first page is "Measures." "Energetically prevent any attempted intelligence activities and access to the zone of operations by members of the UN and UNMOs" and as executors, we have the military police and MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The second entry I'd like to look at is on page 3 of the English, point 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, but would it be possible to also have the original on the screen when we're looking at these? I don't know if it would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We can actually -- we only need the left side of the English translations. That's the key ones. So we can actually keep both vertically divided, yes, if that suits Defence purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Number 5 is: "Collecting and transporting the population trapped in liberated territory in collection centres." That's the measure; and as the executor, we have units of the HVO VP 72nd Battalion. Next item, 6, is: "Discovering, arresting, and bringing in enemy soldiers and officers to the following locations," and locations are listed. Executor units of OG North VP. And the next item is item 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's B/C/S next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Measures: "Prevent burning and looting of facilities in the liberated territory, immediately station personnel of the MUP, special MUP units, and VP in large towns to secure the town and important buildings." The executors here commanders of the OG North units, PD, and VP check-points. Yes. These are the references I wanted to bring your attention to. Now, what's the significance of those entries in relation to the subordination of the MP units to the operational commander?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, these -- these entries mean that the operational commander can give orders to the military police in relation to the implementation of these tasks. This does not rule out that at the same time the military police unit can also receive instructions from the military police administration as to how they will implement these tasks. That second aspect is not visible from this security plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the plan is -- the document is called "Security Plan," or "Plan of Security Measures." What's the significance of a plan in this respect?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on my review of not only the order for attack, but the following orders, the plan -- I mean the word "plan" refers to the fact that it's a schedule, but it doesn't mean to what -- it doesn't mean what we formally understand under plan, like that it's a project. This is not a project. It has been signed by the assistant commander for SIS of OG North; and because of the approval by the commander of the Split Military District, i.e., General Gotovina, it has become an order, and that's also why this included as an annex to the order for attack. I also just like to -- I like to draw your attention to the fact that when you look at the table that's on the right side, okay, we identify measures, executor. That is visible actually on the first page. The third column establishes with whom the executor has to cooperate in order to implement the measure. The timing states, okay, when it is to be done. Very importantly is controls. Controls means here verify. Who verifies or who is entitled to verify the implementation or the degree of implementation of the measure. That's a reflection of command and control doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender 65 ter 161.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections -- Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have no objections, but I would like to raise a question of foundation as it regards to count number 9 referred to special unit police. I would like witness to answer which is the special police meant in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would not mind if he would be asked to explain that, and I do agree with you that it's not an objection which could oppose at this moment admission, but if the witness would know. Now, you said item 9. We are talking about -- we have several series of numbers. Is that on the third page of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is 9, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Since we're already on this topic, Mr. President, I was going to save it for cross, but if he could also explain what he -- why MUP is included there and whether General Gotovina was issuing orders to MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two questions, Mr. Theunens, in 9, which -- the special police in 9, "special MUP units," it says. You're referring to special MUP units, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the one before that, which says "personnel of the MUP, special MUP units" - no comma - "special MUP units and VP." So I'm referring to the the first part of whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Theunens, could you explain or give more details about who were addressed under point 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under point 9, indeed, there, mention is made of special MUP units, as well as civilian police. However, my understanding - and, of course, I base it also on the analysis of the other documents included in my report - is that if units or organisations are identified under "Measures," it has no subordination implications. It is obvious that - and we can see that actually from the other documents discussed in the report - that the implementation of certain tasks will imply cooperation between different organisations. One of the conclusions I draw in the report is that special police units, at least those of the Republic of Croatia, are not subordinated to the military district commander during the implementation of their tasks, and I'm -- I will obviously go into details when we address that specific issue. It is actually the entries in the "Executor" column that are the most relevant in the context of command and control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic specifically asked about special MUP units. Could you further clarify, if you know, what these units exactly are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding, Mr. President, is that this is -- this means the special police, the SJP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic, that answers your question, that it's a reference to -- the witness understands this to be a reference to the SJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry. But just in light of his last answer on Executor, I would call his attention to page 2, column 7, where MUP, is the, in addition to the VP, is the executor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So my question would be, if the witness thinks that General Gotovina was issuing an order to MUP as the executor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, while reviewing or while preparing my report, I have not come across documents indicating that General Gotovina was issuing orders to the civilian police. So it may be that this entry refers to a degree of coordination or cooperation between the military police and the civilian police, as is also visible through other documents discussed in my report and which has been addressed in this trial already, in relation, for example, to exchange of correspondence between General Lausic and Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say that the -- well, let me refrain from my interpretation of your last answer. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to tender 171.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number P1126, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1126 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next document, Mr. President, Your Honours, is 65 ter 5797.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is a short order, one page, by the Split Military District commander, General Gotovina, and it refers to an oral order of himself. He orders in paragraph 5: "Police escort and insurance of the column is to be conducted by the members of the 72nd Military Police battalion, Zadar Company, who will wait for the moving column at Zeleni Hrast." And in paragraph 7, he holds the commander of the TRS-5 responsible for this order, which dates the 2nd August, 1995. Can you tell us, first of all, what the -- who the commander of the TRS-5 is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, TRS-5 stands for "Artillery Rocket Group 5." I know it is based on the 14th Artillery Battalion which at that stage is part of the OG Zadar, so one of the four OGs, but I don't have the name of the commander at this stage. I can try to find it. In any event, it is an order to the commander of the Zadar Company of the military police. The order is not signed by Gotovina. It is signed by somebody else for him. Now, in the military, only the chief of staff is authorised to sign in the name of the commander. The chief of staff of the Split Military District at that time is Brigadier Ademi. That also explains, actually, the first line of the order, "Based on the verbal order of General Ante Gotovina." This is an example of a daily or operational task for the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how does that relate to the issue of subordination?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It confirms the implementation of Article 9 of the 1994 MP rules, as well as the order by General Lausic which we discussed earlier, where the appointment of Major Juric was announced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said that this was not signed, I take it that you wanted to refer to Mr. Gotovina or General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection to the Prosecution adding this to the 65 ter list or its admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm grateful for my learned colleague. I'd like to apply to have this added to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the Chamber should have been more precise in this respect as well. If a document does not appear on the 65 ter list, if it's tendered into evidence, and if there's any objection against adding it to the 65 ter list, I would like to know, and this is limited to dealing with this witness at this moment, so it's not a kind of a general ruling. But for this witness tendered includes permission to add it into the 65 ter list. Objections should include specific reference to objections against adding it to the 65 ter list. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P1127.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1127 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next document I'd like to discuss with you, Mr. Theunens is 65 ter 209, again a one-page order, this time by a Colonel Ivan Vukic. It dates the 6th of August, 1995, and it starts out as follows: "On the basis of a verbal order by the commander of the Split Military District of 6 August 1995, and in connection with the new tactical and operational situation, I hereby order." Then several recruitment issues are ordered, and I'm interested in one, point 5, and I quote: "The joint MP company shall deploy its troops in Drnis with the coordinator of the joint company, Major Zeljko Maglov, attaching one platoon each to the 113th Infantry Brigade, the 142nd DP, and the 15th DP to their deployment areas." What's the significance of this document in relation to the subordination of the military police, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this order follows the situation of the 5th of August, which is addressed on English page 221 in my report, where during which according to a report of the 72nd MP Battalion, the 3rd Company of the 72nd MP Battalion and 4th of the 73rd MP Battalion liberated Drnis as a part of the 142nd HV Brigade. Subsequent to that operational activity, Colonel Vukic, commander of OG Sibenik, whereby the 142nd Brigade is part of OG Sibenik, issues a subsequent order to the joint military police company. "Joint" refers to the fact that it includes members of the 72nd and the 73rd MP Battalion. Major Zeljko Maglov, who is the coordinator for the joint company, is in peacetime the commander of the 73rd Military Police Battalion. The fact that the joint MP company is included in the list of units of OG Sibenik, which are to implement a task, indicates that the joined military police company is subordinated for regular or daily operational tasks to the commander of OG Sibenik, i.e., an operational commander who in his turn is subordinated to the commander of the Split Military District, General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1128, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1128 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next document is 1029, 65 ter 1029.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's an order by General Gotovina, dated 7 August 1995. "In accordance with the need and newly created situation in the zone of responsibility, and in order to have a more efficient organisation and performance of the military police units, I order: "1. The task of the military police and the barrier check-points in the area of Bosansko Grahovo shall be taken over by the military police units of the HVO. "2. The VP unit form the composition of the 72nd VP battalion which has so far carried out the tasks in the area of Bosansko Grahovo is redeployed and shall reinforce the military police unit which is carrying out tasks in the area of the town of Knin." And, lastly, in paragraph 3, we see that: "Responsible for its execution are the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion and the chief of administration of the military police of HVO." We also see who the document is delivered to. Mr. Theunens, the significance, if any, of this document to the issue of subordination?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- Your Honours, excuse me, this order is also discussed on English page 224 part 2 of my report, and it confirms the subordination of the 72nd Military Police Battalion to the command of the Split Military District, General Gotovina, for daily or regular military police task. Also of interest is that this document indicates that there exists another subordination relation with the military police of the HVO, whereby, according to this order, General Gotovina has the authority to issue orders to the chief of the military police administration in the HVO, which is not the situation in the HV.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you explain what the HVO is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO stands for "Croatian Defence Council" and is the name or the acronym used to identify the Bosnian Croatian armed forces, i.e., Croats who live in Bosnia-Herzegovina and who established their own armed forces during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number P1129, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1129 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next document, 65 ter 884, a two-page document in the original, dated 11th August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This an order by General Gotovina, apparently signed for him again, and it reads in the major part: "Due to an increase in requests for sending military police to carry out military police tasks for special interest and importance, I hereby order: "1. The 72nd Battalion of the military police is relieved of its tasks of securing the structures of the command, which they have been securing on the basis of recent orders and a security plan." Again, Mr. Theunens, this order in relation to the 72nd military police, what is the significance in relation to subordination of the military police to the operational commanders?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this order confirms the subordination of the 72nd Military Police Battalion for the regular or the daily military police tasks to the commander of Split Military District. It is also important to notice that securing structure of the command, i.e., command post, is a regular task for military police, but it can also be carried out by other forces. That is exactly what General Gotovina is ordering here. He orders the members of OG Sinj -- there is a renaming of the operational groups around that time period or a reorganisation, whereby the existing four operational groups are restructured into three operational groups, if I remember well. So General Gotovina orders the newly created OGs to organise the security of command post with their own regular forces instead of with the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P1130, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1130 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: There are two last documents in this section. The first one is 65 ter 2062.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is an order again signed for the commander, General Gotovina, 13 August 1995. "In accordance with the need and in order to secure tactical in-depth defence for the remaining or inserted groups of enemy soldiers, I order: "1. Commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion shall urgently send an ATG platoon to the area of Strmica with the task to search and mop-up the general area of Strmica for the remaining or inserted enemy groups. "2. The search of the terrain is to be carried out together with parts of the 6th DP deployed in the area of Strmica. "3. Details of the task will be given to ATG commander upon reporting to the Split Military District command - Knin IZM in Knin." The deadline is immediately. Mr. Theunens, the significance, if any, of this order for the issue of subordination?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's -- this order's coherent with the earlier orders we discussed, i.e., that the commander of the Split Military District, the operational commander in general, can issue orders to his military police battalion, i.e., that the military police battalion - in this case, the 72nd - is subordinated to the operational commander for regular MP tasks. Maybe I can add that the anti-terrorist platoon of the 72nd Military Police Battalion is also at earlier stages used for what I would describe as combat tasks, and I have included such a resubordination record in my report, resubordination order by General Gotovina, a similar order, but dated the 2nd of August. It's on page 211 in part 2, English page 211. And for your information, Strmica is located approximately 15 kilometres north of Knin on the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number P1131, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1131 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The final document in this section is D567 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. I think that's D, is it not? I think it's on the screen as --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I tried to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It came up on the screen as P. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is the analysis of the use of the military police of the OS of RH in Operation Storm, and it's signed by General Lausic, and it dates 16 September 1995. I'd like to refer you to a couple of entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first one is at paragraph 4.1, which is page 6 of the English, at the bottom, and also B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'll read out: "4. Participation of military police units in combat operations in Operation Storm. "At the order of the Split ZP commander, a company of the 72nd VP battalion, which included the anti-terrorist platoon of the 72nd Battalion and members of the regular military police, was subordinated to the 1st HGZ at the start of the operation to liberate Knin and was in the echelon."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Next entry is at page 8 English; page 7 B/C/S, paragraph 6.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The second subparagraph, I quote: "The anti-terrorist platoon of the 72nd VP battalion continued its engagement in combat operations under the direct command of the Split ZP commander and participated in Operation Maestral."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next item is on page 10 in the English and 9 B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph 8 in the English, I quote: "A great contribution to raising the general level of security in the newly liberated area of RH can also be made by the commanders of HV units, from the level of company commander to that of RH ZP commander and chiefs of the HV GS and MORH Administration."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The last paragraph is on page 11 of the English, at the top under number 2, which is page 10 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I quote: "That HV ZP commanders should analyse the proposition of HV units in their area of responsibility, particularly Home Guard units in places where their presence is not necessary, and redeploy them. "Through the Defence administration and unit commanders, update lists of mobilised and demobilised HV members, record the date of demobilisation in the military reserve ID so it can be known who is a HV member and who is not, because many people are wearing HV uniforms and insignia, and we do not know whether they are mobilised." This last quote is from one of the proposals that Major General Lausic added to his analysis. My question to you, Mr. Theunens, is, again, the significance of these entries in this analysis by Major General Lausic to the issue of subordination of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. On this particular issue, and I'm sorry for causing the interruption, but I do think that the relevant portions on that question need to be put to the witness. Page 2, at the bottom in English is, I think, the more relevant portion to that specific issue; and in fairness, it should also be put to the witness. It begins "The combination of the preparation ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "The combination of the preparation, planning, leading, and commanding by the VP Administration and the daily operational commanding by the commanders of the HV ZP and the HV OS made it possible to carry out all the tasks within the competence of the military police and use of VP units in assault operations." Mr. Theunens, can you please answer my question?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the analysis by the chief of the military police administration, General Lausic, dated 16th of September - which I would like to add is also sent to the commanders of the military districts, together, of course, with other addressees, and they are mentioned on page 12 - for command and control is concerned shows that the instructions that exist in the PM Rules in 1994, i.e., Articles 8 and 9, were according to Lausic implemented during Operation Storm. Also of importance is, and I touched upon that earlier, that Lausic specifically mentions that in the zone of responsibility of the Split Military District, military police units, i.e., parts of the 72nd and the 73rd Military Police Battalion, are used for combat tasks. The fact that they are used for combat tasks together with other forces implies command and control for the execution of that task by the operational commander. In relation to the observations Major-General Lausic makes on the issue of security and also the proposals, I see it as a reflection of the duties of the commander, which also includes the enforcement of discipline among his forces, and this applies throughout the operational chain of command. I don't know whether you wish me to comment on the -- Lausic's proposal in relation to the record-keeping for demobilised forces, because I believe that is really not related to command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the documents I reviewed for my report - and if you wish so, I can point at the specific documents - we know that Home Guard units also include people who originate from the areas that were under Serb control prior to Operation Storm. These people, according to the documents I have reviewed, are vulnerable to revenge; not all of them but some of them. This is recognised, for example, by the commanders; not only by the operational commanders but also by, for example, assistant commanders for political affairs, as well as assistant commander for SIS. There is, indeed, a problem also with, as Lausic points out, people wearing uniform, military uniform, whereby it's not clear whether they are members of the military or not. Therefore, in order to be able to establish whether a person in uniform is, indeed, a service member or not, one of the measures that can be taken is to keep proper records of the forces who are demobilised. This is important, because once the forces are demobilised, they do not fall any more under military discipline, at least based on the reports and the documents I have review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you may have noticed that it takes a while to finish the translation, so if you would make a pause now and then and speak a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to move to the next topic, and this is notice, which it's discussed in paragraphs 57 to 65 in the executive summary. So if P1013, page 31 in e-court and page 18 in B/C/S could be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's a large document, so it might take a while to be shown. Let me read out four lines from paragraph 57, starting at line 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's paragraph 57 -- yes, I think it's a later page. I might have misspoken. Not page 31. You just need to move on a couple of pages. Yes, here we are, 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "Prior to Operation Storm, Oluja, General Gotovina is aware that members of the 4th Guards Brigade, 7th Guards Brigade, 81st Guards Battalion, 126th Home Guard Regiment, 134th Home Guard Regiment, and other Split Military District units participant in widespread looting and arson during and after 'Ljeto 95'." Now, in your report, in section 6, you discuss what you call the situational awareness, and that's on page 114 in your first report. Can you tell us the relationship between situational awareness and notice as you define it in your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, situational awareness as such -- I mean, the concept of situation awareness is not defined - excuse me - in HV military doctrine. I found the concept of situation assessment, which is described in the 1993 -- well, I will read out the title: "Instructions on the Procedures Carried Out by the Command Staff on the receipt, issuance, and the forwarding of decisions - orders." This is 65 ter 3382. This is part of the command and control process whereby the commander has to know -- I mean, situation assessment, it's a comprehensive analysis of all elements that might complicate or facilitate the execution of a specific combat order. The relevance of notice is, of course, that a commander has to be familiar with his troops. Not only with numerical aspects like how much soldiers, how many tanks or guns, but also it's the reputation of these troops, their combat readiness, their background. When I talk about reputation, well, certain units may be better trained than others. As I mentioned earlier in relation to the Home Guard Regiments, the composition of units may have significant impact on the manner, how they will implement the mission, and also how they will act or can act once the mission has been accomplished. Therefore, I consider this relevant in the context of -- for the issue of notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to a few documents in relation to notice. The first one is 65 ter 2883, and this dates 15th August 1995, and this is authored by General Gotovina. I'd like to go to English page 7, paragraph 1.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first one, it says: "Military discipline and combat morale in the units was exceptionally high in the preparation, course, and conclusion of combat operations." And paragraph 2.2 discusses, or says, I quote: "Command and control of units was uninterrupted and at the required level." What's the significance in relation to the aspect of notice, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are the conclusions drawn by General Gotovina following a request by the chief of the Main Staff to inform him about what we would call in the military lessons learned during Operation Storm. And in relation to notice, it is relevant in the sense that according to General Gotovina, his conclusion in relation to military discipline is that, as was read out, military discipline and combat morale were exceptionally high during the preparation, the course, and the conclusion of combat operations." This refers directly to Operation Storm, Oluja. The fact that command and control was uninterrupted and at the required level indicates that there were no problems on that level, and that at all times the superior commander, i.e., the military district commander, was in a position to issue orders to his subordinate units, as well as receive information and reporting from these units on the degree of implementation of the orders he had issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number P1132, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1132 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, the next document is a large one in many senses, and I will -- this is the operational diary of the military district. This is P71, and we will discuss quite a few entries. We will start with the English page 43, which is page 22 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And while it's coming up can you explain, and I think you already did it yesterday en passant, what this document is, who compiles it based on your experience, your analysis of all these documents?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, an operational diary is an official document which is kept from the level -- I mean, depending on the army, from the level of brigade onwards. During war, it can also be called a war diary. It includes all the information that is considered important in order to understand the development of the operations, as well as orders that have been given, degree of implementation, as well as minutes of -- or records, I apologise, records of meetings that are held at the command post. The diary is kept in general by duty officers in the operations centre or by clerks they may have, and it's the chief of staff who is responsible for the contents of the operational diary or the war diary. Of interest in this diary, in my view, is that they include detailed records of the working meetings, the daily command meetings that take place at the forward command post of the Split Military District. These meetings -- at these meetings, the commander, General Gotovina, or his deputy, General Ademi, is present and presides the meetings. He will generally start by providing his views on the current situation. Then the members of the subordinate units or other attendees will provide their views on operations they have conducted, proposals they may have for future operations, problems they have encountered, and all other issues that are considered relevant in the context of this command meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to the entry we see on the screen, and if you could always, if you can, indicate which date we are talking about; and for that purpose, you sometimes have to flip back a couple of pages. This first entry says: "VP, military police, they entered Grahovo and they are patrolling the town. The check-point in /illegible/ to assure /illegible/ in Grahovo. The ammunition warehouse in Grahovo burnt down. The army is getting domestic appliances. The security of helicopters in Sinj is OK." First of all, what's the date of this entry and in which context was it made?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we go back to English page 39, we can see the title. If we go to the top of the page, the title is, "Working Meeting." I should have explain the methodology that is being used in the war diary. The time refers to the time of the event, i.e., when the information concerning the event is available or when the event takes place. "Reported by" is the person or organisation who provides the information, and "Contents" is -- corresponds with the information. Here, we have the start of the record of the working meeting at the Split Military District command on the 28th of July 1995, which is one day after elements of the Split Military District have captured or have taken control of Glamoc and Bosanska Grahovo during the conduct of Operation Ljeto. Ljeto is addressed in part 2 of my report, on English page 54. So General Gotovina opens the meeting, and then, as I explain, the subordinates of the units or their representatives address the issues they consider relevant for the meeting. I should also add that such meetings are actually a unique opportunity where all the commanders or their representatives are present, are physically present. They see each other. They exchange ideas. It's also the occasion for the commander, i.e., in this case, General Gotovina, if he has something important to convene that is relevant for all his subordinate commanders, well, this is one of the most appropriate occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go back to that entry I quoted on page 43. In terms of notice, situational awareness of the commander, what's the significance of this entry by the VP?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The significance, Your Honours, of the information provided by the military police is that according to their observations or their information, certain acts are being committed by forces of the Split Military District in Grahovo, and the commander of the military police or the representative of the military police considered -- considers it important for the commander of the Split Military District to be notified and informed of these facts, of these acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would ask for some foundation that these are forces of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No problem in asking him that, although that's a question raised during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But, Mr. Theunens, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned, Operation Ljeto is discussed in part 2 of my report, English page 45. I have relied extensively on the book by General Gotovina, which is introduced as P482. And according to the information I found there, as well as other documents, I conclude that it is the units of the 4th and the 7th Guards Brigade who take control of Grahovo on the 28th of July, 1995. The reference for that are P482; 65 ter 5712; P71, I mean the document we see now on page 35, English page 35; as well as P5697. I don't know, but maybe the easiest thing is to go to page 35 of this document, if we want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I should have been more clear in my objection. My specific objection related to foundation with respect to this specific entry on the 28th of August, that it was at that point in time as a crime being committed by forces of the Split Military District, as opposed to other forces who were involved in the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you address that as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. From the sources I discussed, I concluded that the 4th and the 7th Guards brigade, which are units of the Split Military District at that moment in time, have entered Bosanska Grahovo at 9.40, and, subsequently, the -- I mean, the 7th at 9.40; and the 4th Guards Brigade is at 10.10. I apologise. I agree that the entry -- the army is getting domestic appliances. At first sight or when taken in isolation, it does not allow to draw any conclusions as to which army you're talking about. But from the military point of view, if units of the Split Military District have entered the town we are talking about in the morning, and at the same time the military police -- no, excuse me, if later then that the military police reports that the army is getting domestic appliances, it's not a task of the military police in general to address activities of enemy forces. We have the intelligence officer to do that. So from the sources I reviewed, I concluded - and, again, I would also invite the reader to look at the other entries in the diary - I concluded that the army refers to the 4th, the 7th Guards Brigade, as well as other units, but in any event, units of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, I apologise for the interruptions. I sincerely do. I think there's an issue of terminology here with the witness, which I think the witness will hopefully agree with me on. I was referring to the difference between Split Military District units and the HVO, and not enemy forces, unless the witness is arguing that HVO is part of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should have been more precise, Your Honours. Actually, I should have said forces under the command of General Gotovina, which - and Mr. Misetic is right - did not only include Split Military District but also elements of the HVO. So I thank you for that comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I'm looking at the clock and wondering whether this would be a suitable time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the last break, I said that we have to find a balance. I think we're coming closer to that balance. We will resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue and before I forget, we have a PDF version of the files, report of Mr. Theunens. We inquired with the Prosecution whether there was any Word version available. Apparently, there was not, and PDF files have some disadvantages. Well, since Mr. Theunens provided at least draft reports to the Defence in a searchable format, I think the equality of arms would -- no. That's, of course, between the parties. Is there any way that the Chamber could receive at any moment, and I'm also addressing you, Mr. Theunens, the final version of your report, I'm not talking about any earlier version, in a searchable format, most likely Word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, Your Honours, a Word version of the report; but because during the trial I added the 65 ter numbers and the P and the D numbers, the footnotes have become longer, and, therefore, the layout, i.e., the pagination, is not identical to the filed version any more. If that doesn't represent a problem, then I have no difficulty in providing the Word version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence has converted the PDF file into a searchable PDF format, and we would be happy to provide the searchable PDF to Chambers, if that solves the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the one we have is not searchable. I think that would be preferable above having a version in which other information appears, and may I take it that you would intend to share that to Mr. Waespi as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so that searches may done of the weekend?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's appreciated, the assistance. I don't take it that we make it a form of filing or anything. The filing is the PDF as we have it, and this is just something that assists us in our work. That being on the record, Mr. Registrar, I take it that Mr. Misetic will be in touch with you or with Mr. Nilsson. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just in terms of scheduling, I tried to do my best, but it appears that I won't finish today within these, I think, 5.5 hours originally allocated to me. My sense is that I will need much of Monday to conclude my examination-in-chief. And having --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that. And always what is net time and what is -- I'll ask Mr. Registrar to at least inform us on how much time you effectively used, not being interrupted either by the Chamber or the Defence or whatever, because we usually take net time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let's go to the next entry in this exhibit. This is on page 47 in the English, and I think page 245 B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It has a note at 18.20, "Ademi - meeting," and I quote: "The command-related problems in the units," and then it has the following entry: "The commander of the 2nd Guards Brigade to Glamoc and the commander of the 3rd Guards Brigade in the area of Halapici. Looting and arson reported in the area of Glamoc, Bosanski Grahovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next entry I would like to refer you to is on the next page; in English, page 48, and 25 I think in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The entry in the middle of the English, 1 HGZ: "Entry into Halapic and joining with the 2nd HVO GBR. 20 soldiers from Zadar are setting houses on fire." Then the next entry, a little bit down, Ademi: "The purchases of planks for the units which are setting houses on fire is forbidden." Perhaps also, although it's not directly related but certainly relevant, on the top of the English page: "An order has been given to shoot the legs of all those who are setting fire to the houses and who loot." Comment attributed to the 7th HV GBR. What's the significance, if any, to the notice issue, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, Your Honours, this is the work meeting for the 29th of July, which is presided by the chief of staff of the Split Military District, Brigadier Ademi. We see that the command of the Split Military District, as well as the commands of the subordinate units, are informed of incidents of looting and setting on fire of houses in the zone of responsibility of the Split Military District -- just to correct, in the zone of the operations of the forces that are conducted Operation Ljeto under the command of General Gotovina. I have included the specific order for Operation Ljeto in my report which is 65 ter 2116, which can be found on page 57, English page 57, part 2 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just for everybody's understanding or reminder, what is Operation Ljeto in all briefness?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Operation Ljeto is a continuation of operations conducted by the units of the Split Military District and the HVO in an area known as the Livanjsko Polje and continuing into the Dinara Mountains, whereby these forces are advancing from the wider area west of Kupres. They are advancing along the border between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to capture terrain which, based on my review of the documents, is considered of strategic importance in view of future operations against Knin. There's also a linkage made with the situation of the Bihac enclave or safe area in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And when I say there is also a linkage made, this is, for example, done by General Gotovina in his book "Offensive Operations of the HV and HVO," P482, when he talks about the strategic importance of Operation Ljeto as well as the operations that preceded Ljeto. These operations started sometime in November or December -- November, excuse me, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when was it concluded?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, the Ljeto component, if I can express myself that way, is concluded 28th of July -- I'm sorry, 30th of July. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to next page, page 49, the second entry on the top, reported by 72nd VP. "A warning last night about setting fire to houses. There will be no shooting at Croatian soldiers. In Grahovo, all the soldiers except for the 1st HGZ and 3/1 HVO GBR members took part in setting fire to houses." Let me read the next one as well, "HVO VP": "An order for bringing the VP into Glamoc. There has been an attempt to prevent setting fire to houses. All vital facilities have been insured." Then General Tolj: "The church in Glamoc must not burn down." Who is General Tolj?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolj is the head or the chief of the political administration at the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what is the significance in terms of notice of these entries here in this war diary?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Referring now to the comment or the information provided by the representative of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, and keeping in mind that we know that Grahovo was captured by forces of the 4th Guards, 7th Guards HV brigade, as well as other units, according to the 72nd Military Police Battalion, all these units except for the 1st HGZ - that is, the 1st Croatian Guard which is also known as the Presidential Guards - they were not part of the Split Military District, but for this operation, at least elements of that unit were subordinated to General Gotovina. The 3/1 is the 3rd Battalion of the 1st HVO Guards Brigade. So with the exception of these two units, according to the military police, all other units participated in the setting on fire of houses. Grahovo and Glamoc, they were previously under Bosnian Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And based on your experience of the doctrine, the regulations, why is it significant that General Tolj says that the church in Glamoc must not burn down.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Tolj doesn't specify which church we're talking about. When I say "which," well, Glamoc being under Bosnian Serb control - and if I remember well, there was a Bosnian Serb majority before the conflict, or at least until the operations in Livanjsko Polje - it could have been the Orthodox church or it could have been a Catholic church. One would have to look at the municipal records in order to see which churches exist in Glamoc at the time of Ljeto. Now, if it was the Orthodox church, that could be seized by media, international media, in order to criticise Croatian armed forces or HV for the operations that were conducted there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question in that respect? You give a possible explanation. What about the explanation that one wanted to fully respect the religion of those who used that church? That's another reflection on the same entry. What makes you prefer to tell us that it could have a bad impact on publicity, rather than that it could be that one wanted to fully respect the religious feelings of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course, what I -- the conclusion I drew is one of the possibilities. The reason why I drew that conclusion, but I don't exclude any other options, is that, well, if the setting on fire of houses is generalised or is taking place on such a scale as being described here, that seems to indicate that one wants to change the ethnic make-up in the area. Because why do you set houses on fire? Hopefully, the people living in these houses are not there any more when the houses are is set on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the houses, I mean based on the information included in the war diary as well as subsequent documents, these are not individual or isolated acts of -- you have frustrated or, I mean, isolated soldiers, but it seems that even the most professional units of the HV, i.e., the Guards Brigades, are generally participating in what appears wide scale or large-scale burning and looting. Again, based on my understanding of the conflict and what I've seen before, these activities can have a significant or usually have a significant impact on civilians in the area. There will not be many civilians who will stay when they see that the houses, maybe not their house but all other houses, are being burnt. Maybe the civilians left before, I don't know. Now, of course, Tolj may have intended with his order or his instruction to respect the religious feelings of the Serbs, but the question will be: How many Serbs are still there. So I certainly do not claim that, well, it must be the Orthodox church and it must be for publicity motives; but in the context of the events that we are seeing here, I think it is a quite likely option that the first concern is, well, what will outside observers think of what we are doing, and what will these thoughts or these opinions of these outside observers - I mean by that media or the UN - what will be the possible impact on the reputation of the armed forces or even at the higher level the international position of our country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To what extent do you consider that your expertise allows you to make these kind of assessments, what you consider the most likely explanation in view, for example, of the question of whether burning houses of persons would have any better impact on publicity? I mean, I do understand that if you say, Don't put the church to fire, that a possible explanation among many others would be that it would have a bad impact on publicity. Burning houses, would that not have a similar bad impact, and didn't we see a lot of documents in which concerns were expressed in relation to arson? I mean, you're interpreting this entry perhaps not in a very neutral way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the main reason for me to interpret it in that way - and, again, I don't want to give an exclusive interpretation; I'm just trying to give what I consider the most likely explanation - is a document by -- well, I'm not sure any more whether it was an assistant commander for political affairs or representative of SIS, during Operation Storm. It is in my report, but I have not yet been able to locate it, where - and I'm summarising the report - he states that, "Well, we have been very good at directing the international media towards Orthodox church, which were preserved, and other important cultural or religious symbols of the Serbs. We even showed to the media how a female HV soldier was handing out cigarettes to UNCRO"; whereby, at the same time, the report shows that efforts were undertaken in an organised manner to prevent international media from accessing areas -- or other areas than those authorised by the members of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're telling us is that that report gives some support for your opinion as to the likelihood of this explanation, rather than other explanations. Of course, what I'm concerned about - let me be very frank with you - is that you didn't, say, have difficulties in finding an explanation, but one could think of this which is supported by that or by another. Rather, you just gave us that one explanation and didn't show any inclination to draw our attention that you were talking in terms of likelihood based on considerations which are certainly not fully supported by what was established to be the basis of your expertise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether you agree or not, it's just what I would like to express as my concern. Mr. Waespi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let's move on to page 82 in English; and in B/C/S, it's on page 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first entry I would like to show to you is on the bottom right of page 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's the right side, second column in the English version, please. Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, this relates, as we can see, and I can put that on the record, on page 47, this relates to the 4th of August, and the entry says: "Civilians entered 144th GBR HV and move with the army." Now, based on your analysis of these documents, what is your comment of this entry.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would have to establish --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Counsel, could you just point us to where this is on the screen. I'm having a little difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's on the left side on the screen right now, on the bottom of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Thank you very much. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, one would have to establish the nature, I mean, of these civilians and what their intentions are. I believe that there is a typo or a writing error. There's no 144th Guards Brigade. It's 144th Brigade, so there's not much more I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next entry is on the next page, 83, left column.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just before General Gotovina talks, it says, as reported by PZ: "Morale is good. Knin must not experience the same treatment as Grahovo. Prevent burning and destruction. OG reinforced with PD members." What's the significance of this entry in relation to notice?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the representative of the department for political affairs or political activities who is speaking. He issues, I won't call it a warning, but a piece of advice to all attendees. I mean, this is the report of the working meeting of the Split Military District command at the 4th Command Post on the 4th of August, to say, Look, Knin shall not or must not experience the same treatment as Grahovo, i.e., the looting and the burning. He also adds like prevent burning and destruction, and he says that in the presence of the other commanders, including General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the comment of General Gotovina: "Write an order for the commander of ZM Split and arrest him." What's the significance of that? It obviously doesn't go into notice, but back into disciplinary matters.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this entry has to be seen in connection with incidents that occurred between the commander of the Split garrison and UNCRO troops, and I have discussed that on English page 353 in the second part of the report. I also refer there to the arrest of the commander of the Split garrison on the orders of Gotovina, and this can be found in this diary at an earlier entry for the 4th of August. Yeah, it's the 4th of August in the morning, and I thought it was 9.50, but I'm not able to locate it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you explain briefly without reference to the entry what this is about?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from a later order - and that is 65 ter number 1618, which is discussed on page 353 in the English version, part 2 of the report - this is an order by General Gotovina, where he refers to, I quote: "Based on the most recent information on the activities of the Split garrison and particularly the Split garrison commander," I can read out the name but maybe it's not necessary, "in relation to today's event in Pakovo Selo, I issue the following order." So, during the command meeting, General Gotovina states, "Well, write an order," or instructs to write an order for the commander of the Split garrison and arrests him. This order is then issued on the 5th of August, whereby General Gotovina explains the background to this order and issues a number of instructions. Now, this order of the 5th of August, which is 65 ter 1618, is not specifically mentioned in the war diary here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is that within the authority of General Gotovina to fire the commander of the Split garrison?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is within his authority to arrest him, like to arrest any other subordinate who is allegedly or suspected of having committed serious violations of military discipline, and that can be found in the 1992 Code of Military Discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We will come to that in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next entry, and this is on page 94 in the English and page 56 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for rising to my feet. But if the 65 ter that was referenced by the witness concerning this garrison commander is going to be tendered into evidence, I've looked at it and I notice that there are -- there is a translation error in that document. So before it's tendered, if it could be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then take it that you'll inform Mr. Waespi about your concerns --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and that you'll address them before you include them in your list of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it's already on it when we discuss item number 5. That's tab 46. Thank you, Mr. Misetic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to the right side of English page 94, the bottom. "Minister: The minority steals and destroys the reputation and honour of Croatian forces." Mr. Theunens, what is the significance of this comment by the minister, and do you know who the minister is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to the command meeting of the 9th of August, and we can see that information on page 93. On the same page as there is a reference to an unknown minister, there is also a reference at the top of the page to a Minister Soljic -- or Solic. It was my understanding that he was the minister of defence at the time of the entity known as the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. When you go to the left side of the page, at the bottom, mention is made there of a General Jelavic who was at the time an assistant minister of defence of the CRHB, Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, or so-called Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just conclude on this comment. The significance in terms of notice?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not familiar with the background or the basis for this Minister Solic to make the comments that he makes, but he indicates that he has visited the zone of responsibility, or at least parts of it; and he has made certain observations which he considers important to be known by not only the command of the Split Military District but also his subordinate commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to entry on page 99. Again, it's a Split Military District command briefing, this time on the 11th of August, 1995. In B/C/S it's page 60; English, as I said, page 99, on the left column, bottom, OG Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The comment in the middle is as follows: "Everything is looted. The looting is the problem." Do you know who is reporting that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the command or the representative of the command of OG Sibenik, which is one of the -- at that stage, there are three OGs. I mean, the order for the reorganisation -- the order by General Gotovina for the reorganisation of the Split Military District forces is issued on the 9th of August. But based on the documents I reviewed, it takes a number of days to implement it. So, at that stage, there is still an OG Sibenik. When we look at page 93, we can see this comment is made at the briefing of the 11th of August, 1995. The entries in the operational diary do not allow to conclude whether General Gotovina attended the meeting or not, at least list name is not mentioned among those who spoke at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to the next entry. This is English page 105 and B/C/S 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We see on the top left that this is a working meeting, dated 14 August 1995. The entry I want to focus on is on the second column of this page, the bottom right. PD: "Create lists of officers for all decorations and promotions. Complaint against burning of village Benkovac, /illegible/, et cetera, where there are no Chetniks." Based on your analysis of all these documents, what's your analysis of this entry, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the entry indicates that there has been burning at Benkovac. It's not clear when this burning has taken place. The use of the term "Chetniks," it's not clear whether the term is used for members of the local Serb forces or for Serb civilians. But the term "Chetnik," I mean, has been also used in other instances in the diary. It's not an official name. One could call it a nickname which actually refers to Serb fighters of the Second World War, whereby there was a very violent conflict between, not only with the German occupational forces, but between units known as Partisans, forces of the Independent Republic of Croatia, as well as forces who call themselves Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to page 111 in English, and we'll come to that in the next session in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: General Gotovina: "It's forbidden to burn down houses. This issue is to be resolved urgently." What is the significance in terms of notice, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the entry shows that General Gotovina is aware of the fact that houses are being burnt down. It is also relevant to note that this -- that the burning down of houses, according to this information, still occurs on the 16th of August; whereas, we have also seen earlier entries in relation to these activities. Here, General Gotovina issues a clear instruction to his subordinate commanders at the command meeting on the 16th of August, which can be seen from English page 109.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to the next entry, and this is on page 115 in English and 72 in B/C/S. One moment, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The entry I'm interested in is: "Military police: Control in Otric area. The MP check-point was established. The burning of houses and killing of cattle is being continued." Again, the significance, if anything, in relation to notice, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: These comments are made or referred to the command meeting on the 18th of August, which can be found on English page 114. The information provided by the military police shows that the burning of houses and killing of cattle, yeah, continues on the 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next entry is page 119 and 120 in English. It's B/C/S page 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The entry at the bottom, assistant commander for political activities: "Burning down of houses is a huge problem. The journalists and others who come to visit the area could prove that it was the arson." Mr. Theunens, the significance of this entry?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The significance is not only that the problem which has been existing for some time has been reported sometime at the command meeting, continues to be a problem, but also that members of the Split Military District command, or at least the assistant commander for political activities or political affairs, is aware that these activities can have negative implications, in particular in relation to visits by journalists and, I assume, articles that they might write about these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next entry follows immediately thereafter. It's on the next page in English, page 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "Therefore, I request commanders of the units to take rigorous care in preventing of such incidents in all possible ways. I also appeal the stealing and robbing of properties and cattle to be banned." To whom is this comment attributed?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a continuation of the comments made by the assistant commander for political activities or political affairs. The request he makes falls within the purview of his profession activities, and I have discussed those -- I mean, the role of assistant commander for political affairs, I have discussed that in part 1 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The final entry here is on the same page, attributed to the chief of anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: He says: "As for the issue of houses being burnt down, it's necessary the commanders of units to take care of the area in depth." Yes, Mr. Theunens, what's the significance, if anything, for the issue of notice and perhaps command and control?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of anti-aircraft defence, physically his units will be located in depth. They're not on the front line. His comment suggests - I mean, I cannot draw a clear conclusion from it - so suggests that, in his view, the commanders of units, and I assume he refers to combat units, appear to be more concerned by the situation on the front line, i.e., where the first line forces are deployed and conducting activities, than by the situation in the depth of the zone of responsibility. Each unit will have a zone of responsibility which has -- covers a certain surface. It is not limited to the first line. It also goes in depth. The chief of anti-aircraft defence who, in the concept of warfare is deployed further in depth, wants to share his observations and recommendations with the members of the Split Military District, as well as the subordinate commanders of combat units who are generally deployed at the first line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'm done with this Exhibit P71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to spend two words on further scheduling, but I don't think that we have to bother Mr. Theunens with that. Mr. Theunens, I have to bother you, however, with my instruction; that is, you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, whether already given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back on Monday, the 24th of November. Mr. Registrar, that would be in the morning, at 9.00, in this same could the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Theunens out the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, at the beginning of this session, which was at least at 1.00 today, you had spent a little bit over five hours on the examination-in-chief. So you're approximately at the time you indicated. At the same time, I'm aware that sometimes you are, well, if you would say it very strongly, you were forced to deal with some matters which you may not have chosen to deal with. As far as the continuation is concern, I carefully listened, for example, of course, to the whole of the testimony, but especially the last few questions. You asked the witness what the significance is of entries in a logbook, and then he more or less tells us what it says. He tells us that if someone talks about events, that he's aware of that. Well, you do not need expert knowledge to understand that if someone raises an issue, that he's aware of the issue. Then he says, "Well, this was still the case on the 16th of August." Well, if you were able to read the logbook, you look at the dates, then it doesn't need expert knowledge that this was the case on the 16th of August. Then he tells us it was prohibited to do certain things. Well, that's what the text tell us. It's just one example, but many of these were more drawing the attention of the Chamber to what apparently you considered to be relevant information in this logbook, rather than to rely on expert knowledge of the witness. I'd like you to keep that in mind if you put further questions to this expert on Monday. As always, the Chamber -- I now commented a bit on at least part of an impression of what I had from your examination-in-chief. I'll further discuss with the other Judges on how much time we would still give you. If that would deviate from what you intended to do, we'll let you know, Mr. Waespi. Therefore, it might be important for us to know exactly what you intended to do, how much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think I would need about - and I'll try to focus on the exhibits that haven't been tendered - I would need almost the entire Monday, which means about four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're asking approximately double of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. But as you are aware, I don't know how the calculations were done. A lot of time was spent on methodology and CV and experience, rightly so; but this came out I think a little bit more in the order of the 17th of November which forced me, and I was happy to it, go into more detail. That's perhaps one of the explanations why I needed more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll check with Mr. Registrar whether those times, that is the first 12 minutes you took on the genesis of the report and then the time you took on the other, whether that was included in the little bit over five and a half hours. We adjourn until --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. May I just raise one issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Very, very briefly, Judge. I just had a request on behalf of the Defence, if we have some indication as to the witness's fields of expertise prior to cross-examination, so we could narrow our crosses accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, of course, we have considered the matter that has been raised. The Chamber has decided that it will not set out in detail that we considered the witness to be an expert on artillery but not on mortars, but, however, on ammunition of artillery, yes. I think it may have become clear also from some questions of the Chamber that we take a critical approach to where the witness has specific skills and where his knowledge, skills, and experience might not justify to draw certain conclusions. I'm afraid the Defence will have to do with that. We're not going to delineate exactly this, it is, and that's not. I can, however, tell you that when the Chamber followed, and after having listened to it, discussed the usefulness of saying, here you're an expert, there you're not an expert, and I think we had a similar example this morning, the witness certainly is not a linguistic expert. But, nevertheless, from his expertise we may learn certain matters which are related to other matters on which he may not be an expert, but which are so linked to what he brings to our attention that we shouldn't cut him off just because he's not a linguistic expert. This guidance, I'm afraid - and I also understand that you might have difficulties in focusing your cross-examination and that sometimes you might be a bit uncertain - we have to live with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.
